401.event_title: Bishop Wilberforce argues against Darwin at the 1860 Oxford meeting
401.place: University Museum, Oxford, England, United Kingdom
401.event: At the British Association for the Advancement of Science meeting held in Oxford's new University Museum, Samuel Wilberforce, Bishop of Oxford and a celebrated orator, spoke at length against Charles Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection, published seven months earlier, before a noisy crowd of several hundred. The biologist Thomas Henry Huxley replied, and the botanist Joseph Hooker then rose and, as he reported in a letter to Darwin two days later, argued that the bishop could not have read Darwin's book and did not know the basics of botany. No verbatim record was kept, and the famous exchange about ape ancestry survives only in differing later accounts.
401.explanation: The meeting became a lasting symbol of the gap between confident public eloquence and real command of the subject under debate before a learned audience.
401.tie_back: Like dice moved without a marked board, Wilberforce's polished rhetoric, in the judgement of the scientists present, had no grounding in the science it addressed, so they found no real argument in it to answer.
401._accuracy_note: A strong picture of speaking to a learned assembly without mastery of the texts, but Wilberforce was a learned man in other fields (a first-class mathematician and Fellow of the Royal Society), and the verdict that he lacked mastery comes from his opponents.

402.event_title: Florence Foster Jenkins sings at Carnegie Hall
402.place: Carnegie Hall, New York City, United States
402.event: Florence Foster Jenkins, a wealthy New York socialite whom audiences and critics regarded as one of the worst singers of her day, had for years performed at the Waldorf Astoria and other New York venues, where people came largely to enjoy her mistakes. Urged on by friends, she made her Carnegie Hall debut on 25 October 1944; the recital sold out within about two hours, and she appeared in elaborate costumes she had made herself while the audience laughed and cheered. She died a month and a day later, on 26 November 1944, aged 76.
402.explanation: Her story is remembered as the classic case of a performer whose longing to be admired far outran the ability on which such admiration must rest.
402.tie_back: The kural compares the unlearned man who longs to be admired as a speaker to one who longs to be desired while lacking what desire depends on, and Jenkins's eager pursuit of acclaim as a singer without a singing voice shows that same mismatch between craving and foundation.
402._accuracy_note: A vivid case of craving an audience without the needed basis, but it concerns singing rather than learned speech, and Jenkins and her audiences seem to have enjoyed the performances, so the futility the kural stresses is only partly shown.

403.event_title: George Washington stays almost silent at the Constitutional Convention
403.event: George Washington, whose formal schooling appears to have ended at about fifteen and who never attended college, was chosen to preside over the Constitutional Convention, where many delegates were college-educated men trained in law and the classics. As presiding officer he called on speakers but took almost no part in the substantive debates; according to the record, he first spoke on the issues on the final day, 17 September 1787, to support reducing the number of people each member of the House of Representatives would represent from 40,000 to 30,000. His presence is generally credited with lending the convention prestige and authority.
403.explanation: Washington, who privately described himself as conscious of a defective education, let the convention's legal theorists argue while he presided, and his reputation for judgement rose rather than fell.
403.tie_back: The kural says even the unlearned are counted very good if they keep from speaking in the presence of the learned, and Washington's near-silence among more formally educated colleagues only enhanced his standing.
403._accuracy_note: Washington was self-taught and widely read rather than truly unlearned, and his silence also followed from his role as presiding officer, so the event fits the kural's point only in part.

404.event_title: The Royal Society tests Leeuwenhoek's reports of tiny animals
404.place: Delft, Dutch Republic, and London, England
404.event: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a Delft draper with no university education who knew no language other than Dutch, wrote to the Royal Society in October 1676 describing vast numbers of tiny living creatures he had seen in water through his home-made lenses. The Society did not accept the claims on his word: it asked for his methods, received testimonials from respected Delft citizens, and had the botanist Nehemiah Grew and then Robert Hooke try to reproduce the observations, which Hooke eventually succeeded in doing. Only after this verification was Leeuwenhoek elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1680.
404.explanation: The episode shows learned scientists declining to accept even a brilliant outsider's findings until trained observers had confirmed them, a caution that in this case ended by vindicating him.
404.tie_back: The kural says the wise will not accept the cleverness of an unlearned man as sound, however good it may be, and the Royal Society withheld acceptance of Leeuwenhoek's genuine discoveries until learned members had checked them for themselves.
404._accuracy_note: The Society's caution matches the kural closely, but the outcome also shows that the untrained man's insight was correct, which softens the kural's dismissive tone.

405.event_title: A royal commission tests Mesmer's animal magnetism
405.event: Franz Anton Mesmer, a physician who had moved his practice from Vienna to Paris, drew crowds of patients with treatments based on an invisible fluid he called animal magnetism. In 1784 King Louis XVI appointed a commission whose members included Benjamin Franklin and Antoine Lavoisier; after tests that included what is probably the first blind trial, it reported that the effects came from the patients' imagination and not from any magnetic fluid. Some 20,000 copies of the report were published, the mesmerist movement declined, and Mesmer left Paris.
405.explanation: The investigation is remembered as a landmark in testing medical claims, and it showed how quickly a fashionable reputation could collapse once examined by the learned.
405.tie_back: The kural says the self-esteem of the unlearned withers as soon as they meet the learned, and Mesmer's celebrated standing faded once Franklin, Lavoisier and their colleagues examined his claims.
405._accuracy_note: Mesmer held a medical degree, so he was 'unlearned' only in that his theory had no scientific basis, and his exposure came through a formal inquiry rather than conversation.

406.event_title: Japan's Education System Order aims for no illiterate household
406.event: In 1872 the Meiji government issued the Gakusei, Japan's first comprehensive national education system, which divided the country into school districts and in principle required all children to attend elementary school regardless of sex, family occupation or social status. Its preamble declared that learning was the key to success in life and set the goal that no community should contain an illiterate family and no family an illiterate member. Lack of money, teachers and facilities meant the plan was only partly realised, and it was replaced by a new Education Order in 1879.
406.explanation: The order treated universal learning as the soil from which productive lives and a modern nation would grow.
406.tie_back: The kural likens the unlearned to barren saline land that yields nothing, and the Gakusei rested on the same conviction that only learning makes a person's life fruitful.
406._accuracy_note: A policy rather than a dramatic event; it reflects the kural's high valuation of learning but does not itself show unlearned lives as barren.

407.place: Vienna, Austria, and on tour in Europe and the United States
407.event: Around 1770 Wolfgang von Kempelen presented to the court of Empress Maria Theresa in Vienna an automaton in the form of a robed Turk seated behind a cabinet, which appeared to play chess on its own. For decades the machine, later owned by Johann Maelzel, toured Europe and from 1826 the United States, astonishing audiences. In reality a skilled human chess player concealed inside the cabinet followed the game on a small board and moved the figure's arm with levers.
407.explanation: The Turk became a byword for an impressive figure whose apparent intelligence belonged entirely to someone else.
407.tie_back: The kural compares the fine looks of one who lacks penetrating understanding to a beautifully painted clay doll, and the splendid Turk, with no understanding of its own, was exactly such a decorated figure.
407._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the Turk is a machine, so it illustrates the kural's image of an empty decorated figure metaphorically rather than showing an unlearned person.

408.place: Nauru (officially renamed Naoero in 2026), Pacific Ocean
408.event: Phosphate mining made the small Pacific nation of Nauru, independent since 1968, one of the richest countries in the world per head of population in the 1970s and early 1980s. A major part of the mining income was invested abroad to provide for the time when the phosphate ran out, but the investments lost much of their value through risky ventures and fraud; one notorious venture was a London musical about Leonardo da Vinci, funded by the Nauruan government, that closed within about a month in 1993. By the early 2000s the country was on the edge of bankruptcy, heavily in debt and reliant on foreign aid.
408.explanation: Nauru's story is widely cited as a warning that sudden wealth managed without sound knowledge can leave people worse off than before.
408.tie_back: The kural says wealth in the hands of those without learning does more harm than poverty among the good, and Nauru's fortune, invested without sound expertise, ended in debt and hardship.
408._accuracy_note: Next-best only: this is national financial mismanagement involving advisers and fraud rather than an unlearned individual, and the kural's comparison with the poverty of the good is not illustrated.

409.event_title: B. R. Ambedkar rises through learning to chair the drafting of India's Constitution
409.place: India, the United States and the United Kingdom
409.event: Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar was born in 1891 into a Dalit family, a community then treated as untouchable under India's caste system. He earned degrees, including doctorates, from Columbia University in New York and the London School of Economics, and was called to the bar at Gray's Inn in London. He was elected to India's Constituent Assembly, chaired its drafting committee, and served as independent India's first law minister from 1947 to 1951.
409.explanation: Ambedkar's learning carried him past the barriers imposed by birth to become one of the most honoured makers of modern India, often called the father of its Constitution.
409.tie_back: The kural says those born high but unlearned do not have the worth of the learned born low, and Ambedkar, born into the lowest-ranked community of his society, became through learning the chief architect of his nation's founding law.
409._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural's claim that learning outweighs birth, though Ambedkar went further than the kural by fighting to abolish birth-based hierarchy altogether.

410.event_title: King Sejong creates the Korean alphabet for ordinary people
410.event: In fifteenth-century Korea people wrote in Chinese characters, which were very hard for ordinary people to master, so literacy was largely confined to the elite. King Sejong, the fourth ruler of the Joseon dynasty, had a new phonetic alphabet devised in 1443 and promulgated it in 1446 in the book Hunminjeongeum, The Proper Sounds for Instructing the People, whose preface by the king explains his purpose of enabling common people to express themselves in writing. The 1446 book was inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 1997.
410.explanation: Sejong treated access to letters as something all his subjects should share, opening learning to people who had been shut out of it.
410.tie_back: The kural sets the learned above the unlearned as humans above beasts, and Sejong's alphabet was created so that common people, excluded from letters, could share fully in the human life of reading and writing.
410._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it shows the high value placed on learning, but Sejong's compassionate project sought to lift the unlettered rather than to rank them below others as the kural's harsh comparison does.
